Ceuta Crisis Exposes Europe’s Migration Divide

The EU backed Spain over the Ceuta migrant surge, exposing divisions on migration and Morocco's growing geopolitical leverage.
By
Huma Siddiqui
-
August 3, 2026
Select Preferred on Google News

Instaread

The European Union has refused to suspend Spain from the Schengen Area despite pressure from some member states following a mass migrant influx into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, highlighting deep divisions within the bloc over migration and North African geopolitics.

The crisis unfolded after an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco over just a few days, overwhelming the enclave, which has a population of around 84,000.

Many migrants entered by swimming around border barriers or forcing their way through border fencing, stretching reception facilities and prompting Spain to deploy additional security personnel.

While countries including Italy suspended aspects of their border arrangements with Spain and France tightened checks along its frontier, Brussels opted against taking the unprecedented step of suspending Spain from the Schengen system.

Instead, EU leaders convened emergency discussions to coordinate a collective response to one of Europe’s most significant migration crises in recent years.

Speaking exclusively to StratNewsGlobal, former ambassador Narinder Chauhan, who has served in several European nations, said the EU had resisted calls to politically isolate Madrid.

The “EU has refused to bow to pressures from some member states to expel Spain from the EU Schengen arrangement,” she said.

“The whole episode has exposed the disunity among the EU Member States, some of who are horrified at the prospects of influx of migrants: Italy, for instance, has already suspended its border arrangement with Spain. But the EU head has overruled any attempt to isolate Spain by refusing to expel Spain from the EU Schengen arrangement.”

Chauhan argued that Morocco continues to wield significant influence over European migration policy.

“Morocco holds huge geopolitical influence over EU, operating effectively as its Southern gatekeeper. And uses security-style diplomacy to exploit deep-seated EU anxieties over migration to extract concessions. Morocco’s immediate and potent weapon is the calibrated control over the Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, the only European land border with Africa,” she said.

According to her, “Morocco can tighten or loosen its physical border control based on its real-time strategic goals. The immediate provocation was Spain’s visit to clinch an oil deal with Algeria, Morocco’s arch rival, and opening of the floodgates as a reminder to Spain that playing with both sides of North African politics carries severe border costs.”

Drawing parallels with an earlier diplomatic dispute, she said: “Last time it did so was in 2021 when Morocco similarly retaliated against Spain for hosting a Western Sahara leader, by letting in 8,000 migrants, forcing Spain to give up its neutrality and recognize Morocco’s claim over Western Sahara in 2022.”

Spanish authorities say the overwhelming majority of migrants have since returned to Morocco, but the episode has reignited debate over the security of the EU’s external borders, burden-sharing among member states and the bloc’s long-running disagreements on migration policy.

The crisis has also sharpened attention on the wider geopolitical rivalry between Morocco and Algeria.

Spain has recently pursued closer energy cooperation with Algeria as Europe seeks to diversify energy supplies, a move widely seen as unwelcome in Rabat. Although Morocco has denied deliberately easing border controls, several analysts argue the apparent relaxation served as a political signal to Madrid.

The latest migrant surge has revived comparisons with the 2021 Ceuta crisis, when around 8,000 migrants entered the enclave after Morocco relaxed border controls during a diplomatic dispute over Spain’s decision to host Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali.

Spain subsequently abandoned decades of neutrality by backing Morocco’s autonomy proposal for Western Sahara in 2022.

The current episode has also coincided with broader geopolitical tensions. Some analysts point to recent references by a U.S. congressional appropriations committee describing Ceuta and Melilla as Spanish-administered cities located in Moroccan territory, alongside public support from some Israeli political figures for Morocco’s claims over the enclaves.

However, no public evidence has established coordinated action by any governments in relation to the latest migrant surge.

The political response within Europe has again exposed divisions over migration. Italy suspended aspects of its Schengen cooperation with Spain, France reinforced police deployments along its border, and Portugal stepped up border surveillance.

Several European leaders have also called for expanding the operational authority of Frontex, arguing that the EU border agency should be empowered to respond more directly when member states face sudden migration pressures.
